title: II. Dangerous Witnesses
paragraphs: I don't know whether the witnesses for the defense and the prosecution were sorted into groups by the President, or whether some set order had been arranged for calling them. But no doubt it was. I only know the prosecution's witnesses were called first. I'll say again that I don't mean to describe every single question step by step. Besides, my account would be somewhat redundant, since the whole course of the testimony was gathered up and cast in a sharp, telling light in the closing speeches for the prosecution and the defense, and I took down parts of those two remarkable speeches in full, which I'll quote in due course, along with one extraordinary and entirely unexpected episode that occurred just before the closing speeches, and which undoubtedly shaped the grim and fateful outcome of the trial.

I'll only note that from the very first moments of the trial, one peculiar feature of the case stood out and was noticed by everyone: the overwhelming strength of the prosecution's case compared to what the defense had to work with. Everyone realized from the first moment that the facts were falling into place around a single point, and the whole horrifying, bloody crime was gradually being laid bare. Everyone, I think, felt from the start that the matter was beyond dispute, that there was no real doubt about it, that there could hardly be any argument, and that the defense was purely a formality, and that the prisoner was guilty—plainly, conclusively guilty. I imagine even the ladies, so impatiently hoping for the acquittal of their fascinating prisoner, were nonetheless, every one of them, convinced of his guilt. What's more, I believe they'd have been disappointed if his guilt hadn't been so firmly established, since that would have taken the edge off the final scene of the criminal's acquittal. That he would be acquitted, all the ladies, strange as it sounds, were absolutely certain, right up to the very last moment. "He's guilty, but he'll be acquitted, out of humanity, in keeping with the new ideas, the new sentiments now in fashion," and so on, and so forth. And that's why they'd crowded into the courtroom so impatiently. The men were more interested in the contest between the prosecutor and the famous Fetyukovitch. Everyone wondered, and asked themselves, what even a talent like Fetyukovitch's could possibly make of such a hopeless case; and so they followed his moves, step by step, with rapt attention.

But Fetyukovitch remained a mystery to everyone right up to the very end, up to his closing speech. Experienced observers suspected he had some plan, that he was working toward some particular goal, but it was almost impossible to guess what it was. His confidence and self-assurance, though, were unmistakable. People noted, too, with a certain pleasure, that after such a short stay among us—no more than three days, perhaps—he'd managed to master the case so thoroughly, had "studied it down to the last detail." Afterward, people described with real relish how cleverly he'd "taken apart" all the prosecution's witnesses, tripping them up wherever he could, and, what's more, had cast doubt on their characters, and so diminished the weight of their testimony. But it was assumed he was doing this more or less for sport, so to speak, for professional glory, to show that nothing in the standard playbook had been left out, since everyone was convinced he couldn't achieve any real good by discrediting the witnesses this way, and that he probably knew that better than anyone, having some plan of his own held in reserve, some hidden weapon of defense he'd spring at the right moment. But in the meantime, aware of his own strength, he seemed to simply be amusing himself.

So, for instance, when Grigory, Fyodor Pavlovitch's old servant, who'd given the most damning piece of testimony about the open door, was examined, the defense counsel practically pounced on him when his turn came to question him. It should be noted that Grigory entered the hall composed, almost stately, not in the least fazed by the grandeur of the court or the vast audience listening to him. He gave his evidence as confidently as if he were talking with his own Marfa—perhaps a bit more respectfully. It was impossible to trip him into contradicting himself. The prosecutor first questioned him in detail about the Karamazov family's domestic life. The family picture that emerged was garish and unflattering. It was plain, to both ear and eye, that the witness was guileless and impartial. Despite his deep reverence for the memory of his late master, he still testified that the master had been unjust to Mitya, and "hadn't raised his children the way he should have. He'd have been eaten alive by lice as a boy, if it hadn't been for me," he added, describing Mitya's early childhood. "And it wasn't right of the father, either, to cheat his son out of his mother's property, which was rightfully his."

When the prosecutor asked what grounds he had for claiming Fyodor Pavlovitch had wronged his son in their financial dealings, Grigory, to everyone's surprise, had no proof at all to offer, yet he still insisted the arrangement with the son had been "unfair," that he "ought to have paid him several thousand roubles more." I should note, incidentally, that the prosecutor put this same question—whether Fyodor Pavlovitch had really withheld part of Mitya's inheritance—with marked persistence to every witness who might conceivably know, Alyosha and Ivan included, but got no precise information out of anyone; all of them claimed it was true, but none could produce any definite proof. Grigory's account of the scene at the dinner table, when Dmitri had burst in and beaten his father, threatening to come back and kill him, left a sinister impression on the court, especially since the old servant's composure in telling it, his sparing use of words, and his peculiar turns of phrase, carried as much weight as eloquence would have. He noted that he wasn't angry at Mitya for knocking him down and striking him in the face; he'd forgiven him long ago, he said. Of the late Smerdyakov, crossing himself, he remarked that the boy had been a capable lad, but slow-witted and afflicted, and, worse still, a nonbeliever—and that it was Fyodor Pavlovitch and his eldest son who'd taught him to be that way. But he defended Smerdyakov's honesty with something close to warmth, and recounted how Smerdyakov had once found his master's money lying in the yard, and, instead of hiding it, had brought it straight to his master, who'd rewarded him with a gold piece for it, and trusted him completely from that day forward. He stubbornly insisted the door to the garden had been open. But he was asked so many questions I can't remember them all.

At last the defense counsel began to cross-examine him, and his very first question was about the envelope Fyodor Pavlovitch was supposed to have put three thousand roubles into, for "a certain person." "Have you ever actually seen it—you, who waited so closely on your master for so many years?" Grigory answered that he hadn't seen it, and had never heard a word about the money from anyone, "until it was on everybody's lips." Fetyukovitch put this same question about the envelope to everyone who could conceivably have known of it, just as persistently as the prosecutor had pressed his question about Dmitri's inheritance, and got the same answer from all of them: no one had seen the envelope, though many had heard talk of it. From the very start, everyone noticed how doggedly Fetyukovitch stuck to this subject.

"Now, with your permission, I'll ask you a question," Fetyukovitch said, suddenly and unexpectedly. "What exactly was that balsam, or rather decoction, made of, which, as we've learned from the preliminary inquiry, you used that evening to rub into your lumbago, hoping to cure it?"
Grigory stared blankly at the questioner, and after a brief pause muttered, "There was saffron in it."
"Just saffron? Nothing else you can recall?"
"There was milfoil in it too."
"And pepper, perhaps?" Fetyukovitch asked.
"Yes, there was pepper too."
"And so on. All dissolved in vodka?"
"In spirits."
A faint ripple of laughter passed through the courtroom.
"You see—in spirits. After rubbing your back, I believe, you drank what was left in the bottle, along with a particular pious prayer, known only to your wife?"
"I did."
"Did you drink much? Roughly speaking—a glass, two glasses?"
"Might have been a whole tumbler."
"A whole tumbler, even. Maybe a tumbler and a half?"
Grigory didn't answer. He seemed to see where this was going.
"A glass and a half of pure spirits—that's not bad at all, is it? You might well have seen the gates of heaven open, not just a door into the garden?"
Grigory stayed silent. There was another laugh in the courtroom. The President stirred.
"Do you know, as a fact," Fetyukovitch pressed on, "whether you were awake or not, when you saw that open door?"
"I was on my feet."
"That's not proof you were awake." (More laughter in the court.) "Could you have answered, at that very moment, if someone had asked you a question—say, what year it was?"
"I don't know."
"And do you know what year it is now, Anno Domini?"
Grigory stood there with a baffled expression, staring straight at his tormentor. Strangely enough, it seemed he really didn't know what year it was.
"But perhaps you can at least tell me how many fingers you have on your hands?"
"I'm a servant," Grigory said suddenly, in a loud, clear voice. "If my betters see fit to make a fool of me, it's my duty to bear it."

Fetyukovitch seemed slightly taken aback, and the President stepped in, reminding him to keep to more relevant questions. Fetyukovitch bowed with dignity and said he had no further questions for the witness. The public and the jury were, of course, left with a seed of doubt about the testimony of a man who, while undergoing a certain kind of treatment, might have seen "the gates of heaven," and who didn't even know what year he was living in. But before Grigory left the stand, one more thing happened. The President, turning to the prisoner, asked whether he had anything to say about the last witness's testimony.

"Except about the door, everything he's said is true," Mitya cried, in a loud voice. "For picking the lice off me, I thank him; for forgiving my blows, I thank him. The old man has been honest his whole life, and as loyal to my father as seven hundred poodles."
"Prisoner, mind your language," the President warned him.
"I'm no poodle," Grigory muttered.
"Fine, then I'm the poodle," Mitya cried. "If it's an insult, I'll take it on myself, and I beg his pardon. I was a beast to him, and cruel. I was cruel to Aesop too."
"What Aesop?" the President asked, sternly, again.
"Oh, Pierrot... my father, Fyodor Pavlovitch."
The President warned Mitya again, and yet again, firmly and very sternly, to be more careful in his language.
"You are hurting yourself in the eyes of your judges."

The defense counsel proved just as skillful in handling Rakitin's testimony. I should mention that Rakitin was one of the prosecution's leading witnesses, one the prosecutor placed great weight on. It turned out he knew everything; his knowledge was astonishing, he'd been everywhere, seen everything, talked to everyone, knew every detail of Fyodor Pavlovitch's biography and that of every Karamazov. As for the envelope, true, he'd only heard about it from Mitya himself. But he described Mitya's exploits at the Metropolis down to the smallest detail—every compromising thing he'd said and done—and told the story of Captain Snegiryov's "wisp of tow." Even Rakitin, though, couldn't say anything definite about Mitya's inheritance, and stuck to contemptuous generalities on that point.

"Who could say which of them was in the wrong, which owed the other, with that mad Karamazov habit of tangling everything up so no one could make heads or tails of it?" He attributed the tragic crime to habits ingrained over generations of serfdom, and to the distressed state of Russia, caused by the lack of proper institutions. He was, in fact, given a certain latitude to speak freely. This was the first occasion on which Rakitin got to show what he could do, and he drew real attention. The prosecutor knew the witness was preparing a magazine article on the case, and later, in his own closing speech, as we'll see, quoted several ideas straight from that article, showing he'd already seen it. The picture the witness painted was a dark and sinister one, and it considerably strengthened the case for the prosecution. On the whole, Rakitin's speech captivated the public with its independence of thought and the extraordinary nobility of its ideas. There were even two or three bursts of applause when he spoke of serfdom and the distressed state of Russia.

But Rakitin, in his youthful enthusiasm, made a small slip, which the defense counsel at once shrewdly seized on. Answering certain questions about Grushenka, and swept up in the loftiness of his own sentiments and in his own success, which he was, of course, well aware of, he went so far as to refer to Agrafena Alexandrovna rather contemptuously as "Samsonov's kept mistress." He'd have given a great deal to take those words back afterward, because Fetyukovitch caught him out on it immediately. And all because Rakitin hadn't reckoned on the lawyer managing to become so intimately acquainted with every detail in such a short time.

"Allow me to ask," the defense counsel began, with the most affable, even respectful smile, "are you, by any chance, the same Mr. Rakitin whose pamphlet, The Life of the Late Elder Father Zossima, published by the diocesan authorities, full of profound and pious reflections, and preceded by an excellent, devout dedication to the bishop, I've just had the pleasure of reading?"
"I didn't write it for publication... it was published afterward," Rakitin muttered, oddly rattled, almost ashamed.

"Oh, excellent! A thinker like yourself can, and indeed should, take the broadest possible view of every social question. Your highly instructive pamphlet has circulated widely, thanks to the bishop's patronage, and has done a good deal of visible good.... But here's the main thing I wanted to learn from you. You just stated that you were very closely acquainted with Madame Svyetlov." (I should note that Grushenka's surname was Svyetlov. I heard it for the first time that day, during the trial.)
"I can't answer for every one of my acquaintances.... I'm a young man... and who can be held responsible for everyone they happen to meet?" Rakitin cried, flushing all over.

"I understand, I understand perfectly," Fetyukovitch cried, as if he too were embarrassed, and hurrying to excuse himself. "You, like anyone else, might well take an interest in getting acquainted with a young, beautiful woman who was happy to entertain the cream of the local young men, but... I only wanted to know... It's come to my attention that Madame Svyetlov was especially eager, a couple of months ago, to make the acquaintance of the younger Karamazov, Alexey Fyodorovitch, and promised you twenty-five roubles if you'd bring him to her in his monastic robes. And that this actually took place on the very evening the terrible crime now under investigation was committed. You did bring Alexey Karamazov to Madame Svyetlov—and did you receive the twenty-five roubles from Madame Svyetlov as your reward? That's what I'd like to hear from you."
"It was a joke.... I don't see what interest that could possibly hold for you.... I took it as a joke... meaning to give it back later...."
"So you did take it—but you haven't given it back yet... or have you?"
"That's beside the point," Rakitin muttered. "I refuse to answer questions like that.... Of course I'll give it back."

The President stepped in, but Fetyukovitch announced he had no further questions for the witness. Mr. Rakitin left the witness box not entirely without a stain on his reputation. The effect of his lofty idealism was somewhat dulled, and the look on Fetyukovitch's face as he watched him walk away seemed to suggest to the public, "here's a fine specimen of the high-minded people accusing him." I recall that this episode, too, didn't pass without an outburst from Mitya. Enraged by the tone Rakitin had used about Grushenka, he suddenly shouted "Bernard!" When, after Rakitin's cross-examination, the President asked the prisoner if he had anything to say, Mitya cried out loudly:
"Since I've been arrested, he's borrowed money from me! He's a contemptible Bernard, and an opportunist, and he doesn't believe in God—he took the bishop for a fool!"

Mitya was, of course, reprimanded again for his intemperate language, but Rakitin was finished. Captain Snegiryov's testimony was also a failure, though for an entirely different reason. He appeared in ragged, filthy clothes, muddy boots, and despite the watchfulness and practiced eye of the court officers, turned out to be hopelessly drunk. Asked about Mitya's assault on him, he refused to answer.
"God bless him. Ilusha told me not to. God will make it up to me, over there."
"Who told you not to tell? Who are you talking about?"
"Ilusha, my little boy. 'Father, father, how he insulted you!' He said that, at the stone. He's dying now...."

The captain suddenly broke into sobs, and dropped to his knees in front of the President. He was hurriedly led away, amid laughter from the public. Whatever effect the prosecutor had hoped for fell entirely flat.

Fetyukovitch kept seizing every opportunity, astonishing people more and more with his minute grasp of the case. Trifon Borissovitch's testimony, for instance, made a strong impression—one that, naturally, was very damaging to Mitya. He calculated, practically on his fingers, that on his first visit to Mokroe, Mitya must have spent three thousand roubles, "or not far off it. Just think what he threw away on those gypsy girls alone! And as for our poor peasants, it wasn't a matter of tossing a half rouble into the street—he gave them presents of twenty-five roubles a man, at the very least, never less than that. And how much money was simply stolen from him! And if anyone did steal, he never left a receipt behind. How could you ever catch the thief, when he was flinging money around the whole time? Our peasants are thieves, you know, they've no care at all for their souls. And the way he carried on with the girls, our village girls! They've been living high ever since, I tell you, they used to be poor as church mice." He recalled, in fact, every single item of expense, and added it all up. So the notion that only fifteen hundred had actually been spent, and the rest set aside in a little pouch, came to seem inconceivable.

"I saw three thousand roubles, plain as day, right there in his hands, I saw it with my own eyes; I should think I know how to count money," Trifon Borissovitch cried, doing his level best to satisfy "his betters."

When it was Fetyukovitch's turn to cross-examine him, he barely bothered trying to refute the testimony itself, and instead began asking about an incident during the first bout of carousing at Mokroe, a month before the arrest, when Timofey and another peasant named Akim had picked a hundred roubles up off the floor in the hallway, dropped by Mitya while he was drunk, and handed it over to Trifon Borissovitch, receiving a rouble each for their trouble. "Well," the lawyer asked, "did you give that hundred roubles back to Mr. Karamazov?" Trifon Borissovitch squirmed uselessly.... He was forced, once the peasants had been questioned, to admit to finding the hundred roubles, only adding that he'd returned every kopeck of it to Dmitri Fyodorovitch, "in perfect honesty, and it's only because his honor was in his cups at the time that he doesn't remember it." But since he'd denied the whole business of the hundred roubles until the peasants were called in to prove it, his claim about returning the money to Mitya was, naturally, met with great suspicion. So one more of the prosecution's most dangerous witnesses was discredited.

The same thing happened with the Poles. They took a proud, independent stance; they loudly declared they'd both served the Crown, and that "Pan Mitya" had offered them three thousand roubles "to buy their honor," and that they'd seen a great deal of money in his hands. Pan Mussyalovitch peppered his sentences with a tremendous number of Polish words, and seeing that this only raised his standing in the eyes of the President and the prosecutor, grew more and more pompous, and finally switched entirely to Polish. But Fetyukovitch caught them too, in his snares. Trifon Borissovitch, recalled to the stand, was forced, despite all his dodging, to admit that Pan Vrublevsky had swapped in a different deck of cards for the one he'd supplied, and that Pan Mussyalovitch had cheated during the game. Kalganov confirmed this, and both Poles left the witness box with their reputations in tatters, amid laughter from the public.

Then exactly the same thing happened with almost every one of the prosecution's most dangerous witnesses. Fetyukovitch managed to cast a shadow over every one of them, dismissing them one after another with a certain quiet mockery. The lawyers and legal experts were lost in admiration, though they couldn't quite work out what good purpose it all served, since everyone, I repeat, felt the prosecution's case couldn't really be refuted, that it was only growing more overwhelming and tragic by the moment. But from the confidence of this "great magician," they could see he remained perfectly serene, and they waited, sensing that "a man like that" hadn't come all the way from Petersburg for nothing, and wasn't the sort to go home empty-handed.
